README.md.text:
# VOSTD Code Review

`vostd-code-review` reviews either a Git change or selected Verus source
files against the VOSTD coding guidelines and writes a single, evidence-backed
Markdown report. It covers maintainability, proof engineering and API specification
quality (weak sufficient preconditions and strong faithful postconditions), plus
two conditional workflow checks, in
[`docs/coding-guidelines`](../../../docs/coding-guidelines/README.md).

## Usage

The skill has three modes:

```text
$vostd-code-review diff [<base>] <output> [--overwrite]
$vostd-code-review files <target[:lines] ...> <output> [--overwrite]
$vostd-code-review pr <pr-link> <output> [--overwrite]
```

Examples:

```text
$vostd-code-review diff review.md
$vostd-code-review diff main review.md
$vostd-code-review diff origin/main review.md --overwrite
$vostd-code-review files ostd/src/sync/rwlock.rs review.md
$vostd-code-review files ostd/src/sync/rwlock.rs:120-240 review.md
$vostd-code-review pr https://github.com/asterinas/vostd/pull/860 review-860.md
```

`diff [<base>]` reviews the committed series
`merge-base(<base>, HEAD)..HEAD`, oldest first. When `<base>` is omitted it defaults to
`origin/main`, the `main` branch of the upstream `origin`
(https://github.com/asterinas/vostd); run `git fetch origin` first to review against the
latest upstream main. Each commit's message and diff are captured together so reviewers
can judge the code against that commit's intent. Uncommitted changes are excluded. To
review a historical endpoint, check it out first so it becomes `HEAD`.

`files` reviews the current working-tree contents of the named files, including
staged, unstaged, and untracked target content. Targets use 1-based inclusive
line ranges. Repeat a path to review multiple ranges from the same file. If no
range is supplied, the whole file is in scope.

`pr` fetches the linked PR's head and the latest upstream `main`, switches the current
repository to the PR head in detached HEAD state, then reviews the committed series
`merge-base(main, head)..head`. The comparison always uses `main`. Fork PRs are
supported through the upstream PR head ref. The report records the URL and exact
head/main SHAs, and the checkout stays at the reviewed PR head. Local modifications
are preserved; a conflicting or dirty tracked checkout is reported before proceeding.

In all modes, the output path is the final positional argument and is not
overwritten unless `--overwrite` is present.

## What the review does

The skill:

1. snapshots the commit series or current working-tree target contents;
2. runs isolated reviews for maintainability and proof engineering, plus a
   Specification pass when APIs/contracts or newly verified APIs are in scope;
3. runs a workflow review only when an `rlimit` changes or a `std`/`core`/`alloc`
   external specification is newly added or materially changed;
4. checks important claims against the source, the complete active `vstd`, and existing
   verified code throughout VOSTD;
5. consolidates the results by severity; and
6. writes an English Markdown report containing findings and evidence-check details.

The workflow pass checks only whether a changed rlimit exceeds `200` and whether a
newly added or materially changed project-local external specification for a
`std`/`core`/`alloc` API should be proposed upstream. It does not review CI or host
coverage, toolchain configuration, solver stability, proof decomposition, or other
workflow concerns.

The Specification pass compares documented admissible inputs and promised results
with caller-visible contracts. The LLM inventories APIs, judges contract sufficiency
and checks natural caller scenarios. Device reads can intentionally be unconstrained,
while a mentioned result can still have an inadequate contract.
The procedure is maintained in [`references/specification-audit.md`](references/specification-audit.md).

The LLM autonomously runs targeted baseline/corrected-contract client verification
in a disposable checkout when it would help confirm a finding or validate a fix.
The report records actual diagnostics, fresh verification evidence and material
limitations; unexecuted clients are
labeled as proposals.

In `diff` and `pr` modes, findings must be caused by the reviewed commits. In `files`
mode, findings must be rooted in the named files or requested ranges. The wider
repository may be read as context in all modes.

## Safety and prerequisites

- Run the skill from the VOSTD repository with its Verus toolchain available.
- The working tree is treated as read-only. Only the requested report is written
  persistently; standalone proof experiments run in disposable locations.
  `pr` mode first fetches the review refs and switches the current checkout.
- Existing report files are preserved unless `--overwrite` is specified.
- Review assumes the change has already passed CI. Focused client comparisons run
  autonomously when useful and stay isolated; repository-wide verification is never repeated.

For the complete orchestration rules, evidence schema, and report format, see
[`SKILL.md`](SKILL.md). The aspect-specific reviewer instructions live in
[`personas/`](personas/); the workflow persona is conditional.

SKILL.md.text:
--- name: vostd-code-review description: Review a GitHub PR, Git change or selected Verus files for VOSTD coding guidelines and API specification quality. PR mode checks out the PR head and compares it with upstream main. Checks maintainability, proof engineering and API contracts, with targeted isolated caller experiments; workflow checks cover only rlimit caps and upstreamable std/core/alloc external specs. --- # vostd-code-review Review a Git change or selected code against VOSTD's coding guidelines — primarily `maintainability.md` and `proof-engineering.md`, with two narrowly scoped checks from `workflow.md`, plus API-contract criteria in `personas/specification.md` — and write one Markdown review file. There are three modes: - **`pr `** fetches upstream `main` and the PR head, switches the current repository to that head, then reviews `merge-base(main, HEAD)..HEAD` using the same committed-series pipeline as `diff`. - **`diff `** reviews the committed series `merge-base(, HEAD)..HEAD`, oldest first. Each commit's message and diff are captured so its intent and code changes remain associated. Uncommitted edits are not reviewed in this mode. - **`files `** reviews the current working-tree bytes of the named files, including staged, unstaged, and untracked target content. In `diff` and `files`, the current checkout (`HEAD`) is the anchor. To review a historical commit or range with `diff`, check out its desired endpoint first. In every mode, the question is *which rules does this scoped code follow and which does it violate*, and *can a caller use the API as documented*, with each violation grounded in a cited guideline or API check and quoted evidence. ## Interface ``` diff [] [--overwrite] files [--overwrite] pr [--overwrite] ``` In `diff` mode, `` is optional. When it is omitted the review uses the default base `origin/main` — the `main` branch of the upstream repository (https://github.com/asterinas/vostd, remote `origin`). One positional after `diff` is the `` with `` defaulted; two positionals are `` then ``. Wrap in double quotes any argument containing spaces. - `diff` / `files` / `pr` — **required first positional**, selecting the review mode. - `` — **required in `pr` mode**; a GitHub pull request URL for the current repository's upstream, normally `https://github.com/asterinas/vostd/pull/`. This mode fetches and switches the checkout before reviewing against upstream `main`, including when the PR's declared target is another branch. - `` — **optional in `diff` mode**; any Git ref or SHA. When omitted, defaults to `origin/main` (the upstream https://github.com/asterinas/vostd `main`, remote `origin`). Review `merge-base(, HEAD)..HEAD`; `HEAD` is always the endpoint. Run `git fetch origin` first to review against the latest upstream main; the skill resolves `origin/main` to its current local value without fetching. `pr` mode fetches its own main and head refs. - `` — **required in `files` mode**, one or more targets in the working tree. A target is a path, optionally narrowed `path:N-M,K-L` (1-based, inclusive); repeat a path to add ranges. Ranges for the same path form a union. With no range, the whole file is in reporting scope. With ranges, read the whole file as context but report a finding only when its primary violating location intersects that union; out-of-range lines may be cited only as supporting context. - `` — **required, last positional** (`cp src... dest` style); refuse to overwrite unless `--overwrite`. - `--overwrite` — replace the output file if it already exists. The LLM starts with source review and autonomously runs isolated client/contract experiments when their results could change a finding or validate its correction. See `references/specification-audit.md` for the procedure. ## Repository context Locate these once, before fanning out; the personas need the absolute paths: | Item | How to locate | |------|---------------| | Guideline pages | `docs/coding-guidelines/{README,maintainability,proof-engineering,workflow}.md`, plus `proof-patterns.md` as supporting (non-mandatory) examples. The workflow reviewer uses only `decompose-before-raising-rlimit`'s numeric cap and `upstream-reusable-specs`. | | Existing verified code | The entire vendored vstd tree located from `grep '^vstd' Cargo.toml` (typically `tools/verus/source/vstd`), all of `verified_libs/`, `ostd/specs/`, and Verus-bearing files under `ostd/src/`. | | Verus binary + Z3 | `tools/verus/source/target-verus/release/verus` and `tools/verus/source/z3`, present after `make verus`/`cargo dv bootstrap`; used for standalone logical experiments and isolated spec-client checks when useful. | | Spec audit procedure | `references/specification-audit.md` relative to this skill; API contract analysis and client experiment isolation. | | History rationale | `git log --follow -p -- `. In `diff` and `pr` modes, the captured commit series is the primary review input. | | Default diff base | `diff`: local `origin/main`, without fetching. `pr`: freshly fetched `refs/heads/main` from the URL's upstream repository, independent of local remote names. | ## Pipeline Run these steps in order. 1. **Resolve the input.** Resolve the mode first and capture one immutable review input in a disposable directory outside the shared working tree: - In `pr` mode, perform the checkout procedure below first, then capture the committed series exactly as in `diff`, using the fetched main SHA as ``. Preserve the PR URL, number, declared target, starting branch/SHA, fetched main SHA and checked-out head SHA in the review metadata. Use the recorded SHAs throughout; later PR updates do not change this review's input. - In `diff` mode, default `` to `origin/main` (the upstream https://github.com/asterinas/vostd `main` branch) when omitted, resolve it to its current local SHA without fetching, then record `HEAD`, ``, and their merge-base. Capture `git log --reverse -p --format=fuller ..HEAD` so every commit message stays paired with its diff. Also record the commit IDs and changed paths. Refuse an empty series. Do not include staged, unstaged, or untracked edits. - In `files` mode, capture every target's current working-tree bytes and content hash once. Store each target in a dedicated snapshot file and record its requested range union. Use only these immutable inputs throughout the review. Read each input **in full** before fanning out; do not silently refresh it from a changing worktree. Read the `README.md`, `maintainability.md`, and `proof-engineering.md` live at review start; they are the authority for those review aspects. Read only the two permitted sections of `workflow.md`: the `200` rlimit cap under `decompose-before-raising-rlimit` and `upstream-reusable-specs`. Resolve the repository-context paths above and record relevant earlier history. 2. **Activate personas.** Activate the maintainability and proof-engineering personas for every reviewed Verus path. Activate the Specification persona when reporting scope contains an exec/proof API, its contract, or an API newly brought under verification. Include private helpers feeding that API; no `pub` requirement. The Specification persona decides whether targeted experiments would help confirm a finding or correction. Activate the workflow persona only when the immutable review input has at least one of these changes in reporting scope: - an added, removed, or changed `#[verifier::rlimit(...)]`; or - a newly added or materially changed external specification for a `std`, `core`, or `alloc` API. A material change affects the specified API, contract, model, or panic/unwind semantics; formatting, imports, and comments alone are not material. In `files` mode, determine whether the target changed by comparing its captured bytes with `HEAD` (treat an untracked file as wholly added). If neither condition applies, do not launch the workflow persona and do not report workflow Compliance or N/A entries. Persona activation alone does not justify verification or another expensive experiment; each experiment needs a concrete question whose answer could change the review conclusion or validate a suggested correction. 3. **Fan out.** Spawn the persona passes (see *Spawning*): by default **one isolated agent per activated persona** — best recall. Each pass reads only its own persona block (selective exposure), reviews the target itself, and returns its findings as structured text under the *Evidence contract* below. If all activated passes exceed the available agent slots, queue the remaining pass until a slot is free; retain isolated persona contexts. 4. **Verify.** For each returned finding, isolate the key premise it rests on and try to **refute** it by re-reading the cited code and checking named lemma signatures in vstd/vstd_extra. Check the suggested correction too: resolve its receiver, argument types, trait bounds, and Verus modes, and compare its logical conditions with the original. A valid concern with an invalid fix needs a corrected suggestion; it does not justify retracting the concern or publishing the invalid fix. Do not repeat persona experiments or run additional Verus verification in this step. Assign a verdict: - **confirmed** — keep the finding unchanged. - **uncertain** — keep it, but prefix the problem line with `(unverified) `. - **refuted** — remove it, and list it under `## Retracted by verification` at the foot of the report with a one-line reason. Remove only on confident refutation; an unsure check is `uncertain`, not `refuted`. A guideline finding also does not survive verification if its rule no longer exists on the current guideline page. The Specification persona's `api-preconditions` and `api-postconditions` checks are separately defined by this skill and do not require a matching coding-guideline entry. Resolve cross-persona contradictions (two aspects claiming opposite facts about the same lines) from the stronger cited evidence. If static evidence cannot decide, keep the claim as `uncertain`; do not launch another experiment. Record the resolution in the report's addendum. 5. **Consolidate.** Merge findings that share one root cause into one entry carrying every violated rule's short name. Never drop a distinct guideline violation. Rank the survivors: `high` first, then `medium`, then `low`. Use internal `Compliance` records to check review coverage; omit them from the final report. 6. **Write the output.** (see *Output format*) ## PR checkout 1. Validate the URL and confirm its repository matches this checkout's upstream using remote URLs and GitHub PR metadata. Retrieve the PR head SHA and declared target, for example with `gh api repos///pulls/`. Check the output overwrite policy before switching. Record the starting branch and SHA, and copy this skill directory to the disposable input directory so its personas and references remain available after checkout. 2. Check staged and unstaged tracked changes and any in-progress merge/rebase. If any are present, stop and report the affected paths or operation so the PR review uses clean source. Preserve local changes and untracked files; do not stash, reset, clean or force checkout automatically. 3. Fetch `refs/heads/main` and `refs/pull//head` directly from the validated upstream URL into dedicated local refs such as `refs/codex/review-pr//main` and `refs/codex/review-pr//head`. GitHub's PR head ref supports fork PRs without adding a contributor remote. Resolve both refs to commit SHAs and confirm the fetched head matches the PR metadata; if the PR changed during retrieval, refresh metadata and fetch once more, then report any remaining mismatch rather than reviewing an unknown head. 4. Run `git switch --detach ` in the current repository. Let Git's normal overwrite checks protect untracked paths; if switching fails, report the error and leave those files intact. Confirm `HEAD` equals the recorded PR head and compute `git merge-base `. Fetch missing history if a shallow checkout prevents resolving that merge-base; report unresolved failures. 5. Continue the diff pipeline using those immutable SHAs. Read project guidelines and surrounding source from the PR checkout; use the captured copy of this skill for orchestration. Leave the checkout at the reviewed PR head and state that head and the main SHA in the report and completion message. ## Spawning a persona pass Launch passes in parallel up to available capacity with a no-history isolated fork (`fork_turns: "none"`, or the environment's exact equivalent). Do not use the default conversation-inheriting fork: each pass receives only its persona and the explicit context below. Each pass prompt is built the same way: 1. the persona file's full text (`personas/.md`), verbatim, as the stable head; 2. the absolute paths of the repository-context table (guideline pages, existing verified-code roots, Verus binary, verification-gate configuration, branch); 3. the mode and immutable review input: in `diff` or `pr` mode, the absolute captured-log path, merge-base, HEAD, commit IDs, and changed paths; in `files` mode, each original target path plus its absolute snapshot path, content hash, and reporting ranges. Do not embed source or diff contents in the prompt. Pass rules stated in every prompt: - Read the immutable review input from the supplied paths; do not replace it with live Git output or working-tree files and do not rely on summaries. Maintainability and proof-engineering reviewers read their full guideline page; the workflow reviewer reads only the two permitted rule sections named in its persona. The Specification reviewer reads its own criteria and the linked audit procedure, plus its named supporting guideline sections. The live repository may be read only for surrounding context and verification. Report locations using original paths and source line numbers, never disposable paths. - Enforce reporting scope. In `diff` or `pr` mode, a finding's primary violating location must be introduced or materially changed by a reviewed commit; removed code may support a finding about the resulting change. Bringing a previously unverified API under verification counts as a material change even if its body is unchanged: cite the original API location and the changed enclosing macro/attribute as scope evidence. In `files` mode, the primary location must intersect the target's requested range union. Context outside the scope cannot create an independent finding. Scope Compliance claims the same way. - For maintainability and proof engineering, the guideline page outranks the persona file's method list: enumerate and check every current rule. The workflow persona is the explicit exception: check only the triggered `rlimit > 200` condition and/or whether a newly added or materially changed `std`/`core`/`alloc` external spec should be proposed upstream. Do not inspect or report any other workflow concern. - The Specification persona is another focused exception: check its two API criteria rather than enumerating a full guideline page. Its findings may cite the skill-defined `api-preconditions` or `api-postconditions` IDs. - A method may only propose a finding; a finding stands only if a permitted guideline or the Specification persona's API criteria ground it. For maintainability and proof engineering, if a page rule fits no method, design the check on the spot and keep the finding format. - Apply guidelines within Rust/Verus semantics. A style rule cannot justify weakening a contract, adding an unsupported trait bound, or assuming a type invariant for an arbitrary spec value. If guideline wording would require such a change, record the guideline ambiguity in the evidence check record rather than reporting that change as a required fix. - Check each concrete suggestion against the actual signature and original logical conditions. In particular, `x matches Some(v) ==> P(v)` accepts `None`; preserve any existing `x is Some` requirement. Resolve the receiver that owns a reused predicate and distinguish `P` from `Option

` before suggesting a replacement. Distinguish a demonstrated violation from a valid concern whose proposed fix needs correction. - A finding exists only with quoted evidence — code lines, comment lines, command output, or named lemma/spec signatures checked in vstd/vstd_extra. State unknown facts as unknown. - Cite every violation by the guideline's kebab-case short name (`docs/coding-guidelines/README.md`) or one of the two explicit API check IDs. - Classify a finding by its suggested action. A finding whose correction is to write or reword documentation or comments (`document-verified-apis`, `document-real-proof-debt`) is reportable only when the missing or wrong text would mislead a reviewer about verified behavior or a trust boundary — a missing or contradicting trusted-boundary/`Safety` statement for a newly introduced verified API, or a doc claim inconsistent with the contract. Completeness-only documentation findings — enumerating trivial clauses the signature or ordinary rustdoc already states, bullets not mirroring every conjunct, retrofitting a module-level paragraph onto code whose verification grew in the diff, wording or format polish — are not findings; mention them at most once under `Compliance`. A reportable documentation finding is always `low`. - Include a `Compliance` list of rules the code demonstrably follows, with line references. - You may run read-only repository commands and standalone experiments in a disposable directory. Never edit, back up, restore, or construct modified variants of files in the shared working tree. - Exhaust the static checks first (reading, grep, git history); every experiment must be able to name the report outcome it can change — run none whose outcome changes nothing. - Do not repeat CI verification. Standalone proof experiments checking a specific logical premise remain allowed. The only focused/module or controlled-variant exception is the Specification persona's autonomous targeted experiments, following `references/specification-audit.md` in a disposable checkout. Repository-wide verification remains excluded, and no experiment may edit the shared working tree. - Return exactly the structured data defined by the *Evidence contract* below, with no surrounding prose. ## Evidence contract Every persona returns one YAML-shaped block with exactly two keys: `Findings` and `Compliance`. `Compliance` is an internal review-coverage record. Keep every field; use `null` or `[]` rather than omitting an unknown or empty value. ```yaml Findings: - id: - severity: high | medium | low guideline: location: quoted_evidence: problem: key_premise: experiment: attempted: true | false command: exit_code: result: suggestion: Compliance: - guideline: status: complies | not-applicable locations: [, ...] quoted_evidence: compliance_or_na_reason: ``` For Specification, cover both API check IDs under `Findings` or `Compliance`. For maintainability and proof engineering, each current rule from the persona's guideline page appears at least once under either `Findings` or `Compliance` — a rule with no violation appears under `Compliance` only; never surface a manufactured finding to clear the list. For workflow, include only the applicable triggered check(s); omit all non-triggered and all other workflow rules rather than recording N/A entries. Findings use a primary location inside the requested diff or file/range scope; out-of-scope support stays inside `quoted_evidence`. Commit messages may establish intent but are not independently reviewed for style unless a current VOSTD guideline explicitly requires it. Do not assign the orchestrator's `confirmed` / `uncertain` / `refuted` verdict in persona output. ## Output format One Markdown file: ```markdown # Review: (branch ) > Produced from docs/coding-guidelines and the skill's API-contract criteria; > CI verification is a review precondition. > Scope: <`pr main= head= merge-base= []`, > `diff .. []`, or > `files captured from the working tree; = []`>. **Bottom line:** two to five sentences naming the single most important problem. ## High (one `###` per finding) ## Medium (one `###` per finding) ## Low (one row per finding: Finding | Guideline | Detail; merge rows sharing one guideline and root cause) ## Retracted by verification (only if any) ## Addendum: cross-persona resolution (only if any) ## Evidence check record (static, standalone and targeted spec-client evidence) ``` Every finding states: the guideline short-name or API check ID, location (`file:line`), the quoted evidence, the problem in one or two sentences, and a concrete suggestion. Severity: `high` = a reviewer would block the PR on it; `medium` = should be fixed before merge; `low` = nit or readiness note. The report is always in English. ## Ground rules - The review stays delegated: one sub-agent per activated persona; the orchestrator synthesizes but does not review inline. - Treat the existing working tree as read-only. The only persistent file this skill writes there is ``; experiment artifacts belong in a disposable directory outside it and must not alter or restore user files. In `pr` mode, the PR checkout step additionally fetches review refs and switches `HEAD` as described above; the review itself remains read-only.

references/specification-audit.md.text:
# API specification audit

Use this procedure to evaluate API contracts and validate findings with natural
caller scenarios.

## Source analysis

Read scoped APIs, documentation, contracts and callers. Evaluate input admissibility
and meaningful guarantees for every scoped API, including those with populated
postconditions. Inspect macro definitions, attributes and trait contracts where
relevant. Record unresolved facts and generated-item limitations in the report.

Capture function identity, original source span, mode, visibility, verification and
trust status, callable trait/impl contract, return value and mutable outputs. In
`diff` and `pr` modes include functions intersecting changed lines and functions newly
brought into verification by a surrounding macro/attribute/module change. De-duplicate by function
identity, not line count. Supporting callees outside scope cannot become findings.

For each output, inspect `ensures`, `returns`, attribute desugaring and inherited
contracts. Check that callers can establish the next operation's obligations using
the available guarantees, return types and accessible invariants. Identify missing
facts and conditions that constrain only a trivial property, the wrong state or a
vacuous implication. Check effects such as global initialization and ownership
transfer, including functions that return unit.

Evaluate each candidate against the documented behavior and give evidence. Device
reads may genuinely yield arbitrary values; masked reads can still promise bounds
and alignment. Do not equate preserving a wrapper's fields with preserving hardware
state. Prefer abstract frame facts over whole-object equality unless equality is
both justified and appropriate to the abstraction. Check preconditions against the
documented input domain and the caller's available permissions and state.

## Targeted client experiments

The LLM decides whether an experiment could confirm or refute a finding, resolve a
material uncertainty, or validate a suggested correction, then runs it autonomously.
Name the question and how the result would affect the review before running an
experiment. Skip experiments that would add no useful evidence. Record tooling
limitations when they affect a conclusion.

Use scoped contract/client verification in a disposable checkout outside the shared
working tree. This does not permit repository-wide verification, publishing changes,
changing the user's files or adding assumptions/trusted bodies.

1. Materialize the recorded review endpoint in an isolated checkout. For `files`
   mode overlay the captured target bytes and capture any required working-tree
   context; record those hashes. Preserve the original shared checkout and index.
   Use the configured toolchain and separate build artifacts; do not bootstrap or
   upgrade a toolchain as part of a review. If isolation or dependencies are unavailable,
   record the limitation and retain the static result.
2. Write a minimal client from a documented use or real caller, at the same module
   visibility and abstraction boundary. Establish legal, satisfiable preconditions.
   Do not let a client unfold a private body unavailable to its modeled caller or
   strengthen its premises with the fact under investigation. Record adaptations
   and the limits they place on what the experiment establishes.
3. Verify baseline plus client, then the identical client with the minimal candidate
   contract correction and required proof-only support. For excessive `requires`,
   test the relaxed contract against its implementation too. Avoid executable edits;
   if the correction would require one, record a proposed change and limitation
   rather than silently incorporating it into a spec-only experiment.
4. Check that baseline failure is the named obligation, not a parse, visibility,
   unsupported feature or unrelated model failure. Check the corrected implementation
   as well as its client. Strengthening an external contract can make the client pass
   without establishing soundness; document that trust separately. Do not conclude
   repository-wide compatibility from a local pass.
5. Record exact commands, source hashes, toolchain, exit codes, verification counts
   and relevant diagnostics for each variant. Require fresh verifier output: changing
   focus flags or touching a file may only hit cargo-verus caches. A cached `Verified`
   banner is not a new check. Use the supported rebuild mechanism in isolation if
   needed; never clear the shared build cache. If freshness remains uncertain, say so.
   Use a deliberately false contract in a separate disposable variant only when
   necessary to resolve whether a contract was checked. It should fail for the
   expected obligation; it must never become part of the proposed patch.

Stop after the selected premise is resolved or a concrete tooling limitation is
established. Findings need evidence, not repeated solver runs. The orchestrator
checks the recorded evidence without rerunning the persona's experiments.

Return findings and experiment evidence using the shared evidence contract. Include
material unresolved limitations in the evidence check record.

personas/specification.md.text:
# Specification persona

**Remit:** Can a natural caller use the API for its documented purpose, with no
unnecessary obligations and with all meaningful promised results available?

Read the target's rustdoc, contracts, implementation, trait declarations and
relevant callers. Read `references/specification-audit.md` relative to this skill
for contract analysis and targeted client experiments.
Read the `complete-external-contracts` and `implement-inv-for-models` sections of
`docs/coding-guidelines/proof-engineering.md` as supporting semantic constraints.
Evaluate contract quality and report evidence-backed findings, running targeted
experiments when useful.

## Review criteria

Use these two skill-defined check IDs in the evidence contract's `guideline` field.

- **`api-preconditions`:** Make `requires` as weak as soundness and documented
  behavior permit. For each clause, identify its role: safety, protocol ownership,
  valid state, non-panicking regime, or a genuine semantic restriction. Look for
  excluded documented inputs, conditions that demand an outcome instead of accepting
  an input, implementation-specific constraints, and obligations callers cannot
  obtain from the public abstraction. Give a concrete documented legal call that a
  suspect clause excludes, or demonstrate that the clause is redundant. Keep real
  bounds, permissions, initialization, architecture and aliasing requirements.
  A safe fallible API may accept an invalid request and return `Err`/`None`; do not
  require success as an input merely to simplify proof. Conversely, do not remove a
  non-panicking precondition without checking the API's promised panic semantics.
  Classify undocumented necessary restrictions as a contract/documentation conflict;
  do not assume the implementation can soundly accept every undocumented input.
- **`api-postconditions`:** Make `ensures`/`returns` as strong as the documented
  abstract behavior justifies. Check result values, success/failure conditions in
  both directions where promised, initialized state and identity, ownership effects,
  frame conditions for mutable arguments, and preserved relationships needed for
  the next natural API call.
  Prefer exact abstract results for deterministic getters and constructors; preserve
  nondeterminism for hardware, concurrency, and opaque external APIs. Do not expose
  private representation or freeze incidental implementation choices just to obtain
  a stronger formula. Propose the strongest useful abstract guarantee supported by
  the API, not every provable detail of its body.
  Output-position coverage discipline: pin every output — return values
  (including named binders `res/r =>` and `returns` exact shapes), the final
  state of every exec or tracked `&mut` argument (`final(p)`/`*final(p)`,
  both Ok and Err arms), `&mut self` via `final(self)`, and arrow-form ghost
  out-params (`with -> name: Tracked<T>`; value-consumption form `with
  Tracked(x)` is an input, not an output). A diverging `-> !` function has no
  return-position obligation. Mentioning only `old(p)`, only a negated or
  projected fragment of an output, does not pin it.
  Strength caveats: an `ensures /* */` empty attr text or a vacuously
  inherited contract (`obeys false`) is coverage in name only; a trait-impl
  inherits the declaration's strength, so when the declaration itself misses
  an output, anchor the finding at the trait declaration — one fix at the
  declaration heals every impl site, and a per-impl patch heals nothing.
  Exemption boundaries: a bare zero-clause constructor is exempt, one with
  `requires` is not; a one-hop pure reader is getter-exempt, multi-hop or
  side-effecting readers are not; plain-Rust scope findings are
  severity-capped, never ignored.

## Method

1. Inventory scoped exec/proof APIs and their outputs, including private helpers
   that feed those APIs. Include newly verified functions whose bodies did not
   change, trait contracts, generated items and trusted boundaries when relevant.
2. Map documentation to input obligations and output guarantees. Inspect the
   callable contract (including trait/inherited/attribute contracts), not just
   textual `ensures`. Check return values and the final state of every `&mut`
   argument, including functions returning unit and tracked outputs.
3. Trace missing guarantees into a natural caller's next obligation, or cite the
   documented promise the contract fails to expose.
4. Refute candidates with existing contracts, legal type-invariant facts, return
   types, and other accessible evidence. Arbitrary spec values do not inherit type
   invariants. A concrete implementation's stronger contract is not automatically
   available through a trait call. Preserve `Some` requirements, receiver types,
   and all required ownership conditions in suggested replacements.
5. Separate value correctness, conditional coverage and termination. A closure's
   return-value `ensures` does not prove it returns; a finite model of remaining
   items does not establish production or completion. Consult the active iterator
   contract to determine which guarantees are available. A missing
   dependency guarantee may be a limitation, not a defect this API must fix by
   rewriting executable code or introducing trust.
6. Run client experiments when they could confirm or refute a finding,
   resolve a material uncertainty, or validate a suggested correction.
   Skip experiments whose outcome would not affect the review. Record limitations
   that affect a conclusion, and describe unexecuted clients as proposals. Use the
   reference's isolation and evidence requirements.

## Findings and boundaries

Every finding needs a documented promise or justified caller use, the precise
missing/excessive clause, quoted source, and a concrete correction. Distinguish
current verified callers from unverified startup code, commented-out clients and
future integration examples. Lack of a current caller does not excuse a missing
explicit API promise, but future-only usability gaps are not current verification
failures. Rank impact accordingly; do not assign blocking severity merely because
a diagnostic client fails.

An acknowledged trust boundary is not automatically harmless or a new finding: check it against the
documented promise and report a concrete contradiction if present. Documentation
wording-only fixes belong to Maintainability; a missing formal guarantee is a
semantic contract issue even if its evidence comes from rustdoc. Do not resolve
such a gap by silently weakening the documentation.

Return the shared `Findings` and `Compliance` block. Cover both check IDs with
findings or internal compliance notes.
Proof Engineering owns external-model soundness, vacuity, model choice and reuse;
you own API input admissibility and caller-visible guarantee sufficiency. Shared
root causes are merged by the orchestrator, not reported twice.

# Workflow persona

**Review section:** findings on excessive rlimits and upstreamable standard-library
external specifications

**Remit:** Perform only the triggered checks below. Do not review host coverage,
toolchain configuration, solver stability, proof decomposition, CI configuration, or
any other workflow concern.

Read only the relevant text of these two rules in
`docs/coding-guidelines/workflow.md`:

- `decompose-before-raising-rlimit`, solely for its `rlimit <= 200` threshold;
- `upstream-reusable-specs`, solely to decide whether a changed project-local external
  specification should be proposed to upstream Verus.

## Checks

1. For every added, removed, or changed `#[verifier::rlimit(...)]` in reporting scope,
   inspect the new value. Report a finding under `decompose-before-raising-rlimit` only
   when the new value is greater than `200`; otherwise record compliance. Do not judge
   whether the rlimit is necessary, whether the proof should be decomposed, or any
   other solver setting. A removed rlimit complies.
2. For every newly added or materially changed external specification for a `std`,
   `core`, or `alloc` API in reporting scope, decide whether it is generally reusable
   beyond VOSTD. A material change affects the specified API, contract, model, or
   panic/unwind semantics; formatting, imports, and comments alone do not qualify.
   Report a finding under `upstream-reusable-specs` when a generally reusable
   project-local specification should be proposed upstream and the review input does
   not record that plan; otherwise record compliance. Do not expand this into contract
   correctness, caller validation, dependency, placement, or repository-wide reuse
   checks; those belong elsewhere.

Return entries only for checks actually triggered by the immutable review input. Do
not enumerate the workflow guideline page and do not emit N/A entries for untriggered
or excluded rules.

personas/proof-engineering.md.text:
# Proof-engineering persona

**Review section:** High/Medium/Low findings on contracts, trust, and models
**Remit:** Is every caller-visible contract stateable and dischargeable,
is every trusted fact stated at the right boundary,
and is every model the simplest one that already exists?

**Your guideline page (the authority — read it in full first):**
`docs/coding-guidelines/proof-engineering.md`

Open the page now and enumerate every rule it currently contains, by kebab-case short
name. Check every one of them against the target; the page outranks everything below.
If the page has rules this list does not name, review them through the closest method
below; if a rule named below no longer exists on the page, drop it. `proof-patterns.md`
records recurring VOSTD proof shapes as supporting examples, not mandatory rules — never
report a finding merely because the code diverges from a pattern.

**Concerns, in order:**

1. Take the page's current rule list as your checklist; clear every rule with a finding
   or an explicit compliance note citing line references.
2. Contract-completeness sweep (`complete-external-contracts`). Enumerate every trusted
   external specification the proof relies on (imports from `vstd_extra::external`, and
   non-`pub` vstd items the proof unfolds). For each, check against the exact dependency
   version's source, API docs, and comments: equivalence clauses are bidirectional; the
   direction of each axiom and spec impl actually supplies the direction the proof needs
   (a missing converse is a gap); preconditions, postconditions, well-formedness, and
   panic/`no_unwind` claims match what the spec promises, with documented panic conditions
   excluded by explicit preconditions rather than a bare `may_panic`; closure-driven
   adapters require the closure's per-element preconditions only where invoked and promise
   neither termination nor `no_unwind` unless the contract requires the closure to
   terminate and not panic; size bounds use the library's real representation limits
   (e.g. `usize::MAX / 8`, not just `usize::MAX`).
3. Vacuity check (`complete-external-contracts`). For `ensures ... <antecedent> ==> ...`
   clauses the target introduces, first inspect verified lemmas and real callers that
   establish the antecedent. A failure to prove the antecedent at the definition site is
   not evidence of vacuity: callers may have stronger facts. Confirm vacuity only when a
   checked argument shows that, under the original `requires`, the antecedent is false for
   every legal call (for example, a faithful standalone proof of `!<antecedent>` from those
   preconditions). Preserve all relevant definitions and trusted assumptions in a
   standalone experiment, run it with the repository Verus binary (`--crate-type lib`,
   `VERUS_Z3_PATH` set to the vendored z3), and try to refute the claim with a legal
   witness or caller before reporting it. If real callers merely cannot establish the
   antecedent, report a caller-usability or contract-completeness gap instead of vacuity;
   choose severity from its impact rather than assigning `high` automatically. Also list
   unconditionally provable facts missing from the contract. For a closure carrying
   `#[verus_spec(...)]`, distinguish ambient facts legitimately used to establish a
   self-contained closure contract at construction from obligations that future invocations
   need. Report a finding only when the caller-visible closure contract omits such a
   required obligation.
4. Trust-boundary sweep (`centralize-trusted-boundaries`, `restrict-generic-trusted-models`).
   Grep the target for `assume|admit|external_body|uninterp|broadcast axiom|axiom`; a
   trusted fact kept beside a caller instead of in `vstd_extra::external` is a finding.
   Prefer `assume_specification` matching the original generic signature, trait bounds, and
   associated types; before adding an external function wrapper, test the direct form with
   the active toolchain and record any concrete obstacle. Note unused or superseded helpers
   in the boundary modules the target points at. When a trusted model is generic, trait
   bounds and external trait declarations do not by themselves establish its semantic laws:
   inspect associated types, aliasing, and interior mutability, and guard its guarantees
   with a model-validity predicate admitted only for reviewed type and architecture
   combinations (e.g. the immutable `Seq<bool>` model for `bitvec` is limited to storage
   `u8`/`u32`/`usize`/`u64` on 64-bit targets with `Lsb0`; `BitStore` alone is insufficient
   because some implementations mutate through shared references). If the external
   signature must stay generic, the validity predicate must name the relevant storage,
   ordering, and index types.
   Do not infer a missing `S: Send` bound just from `unsafe impl<S> Send` or
   `PhantomData<S>`. Trace actual runtime storage, captures, constructor bounds
   (including supertraits), destruction, and invocation. Distinguish an actual stored
   `S` or queued certificate from a marker and a separately supplied invocation-time
   `Tracked<S>`. A manual `Send` impl may be justified by `C: Send + 'static`, private
   paired construction, and consuming dispatch even when automatic trait derivation
   would impose `S: Send`. A missing-bound finding needs a concrete unsafe transfer
   or access path not excluded by those constraints; phantom or erased parameters
   alone establish neither soundness nor unsoundness. See the
   [retracted PR #860 finding](https://github.com/asterinas/vostd/pull/860#discussion_r4396503947).
5. Reuse sweep (`reuse-existing-specifications`). Inventory every spec fn, proof fn,
   lemma, axiom, model, and external specification introduced or materially changed in
   the reporting scope. Search for equivalent semantics and signatures across all active
   verified-code roots, not a hand-picked file list:
   - the entire vendored `vstd` source tree;
   - all of `verified_libs/`, including `vstd_extra`;
   - `ostd/specs/`; and
   - other Verus-bearing files under `ostd/src/`.
   Before modeling a standard-library API that `vstd` does not yet cover, also check the
   Verus upstream for accepted or in-progress models, and reuse or wait rather than fork a
   competing local spec (a second trust source causes model drift). Batch name and
   signature searches across these roots, then inspect semantic candidates even when their
   names differ. Report a duplicate only with quoted signatures or definitions showing the
   overlap; name similarity alone is not evidence. Prefer the existing verified operation
   (e.g. `saturating_add`) or extend the narrowest reusable layer instead of adding an
   overlapping local model. When a checked proof replaces an `assume`/`admit`/`=~= cheat or
   a bridge lemma, call the verified fact directly and remove the cheat so the trusted
   surface net-shrinks. Also flag restated postconditions that merely unfold the lemma's
   own `requires` and inflate the SMT goal for every downstream lemma.
   Validate a reuse suggestion in the caller's actual signature: identify the receiver
   owning the predicate, its visibility and mode, and each argument's type. Preserve
   the original conditions when factoring the predicate.
6. Model-choice review (`canonical-spec-models`, `distinguish-spec-and-exec-indexing`,
   `quantifiers-and-triggers`). Is each model the simplest standard mathematical type
   (`Range<int>` for an integer range, `Map` for a map view, a sequence plus a position for
   an ordered cursor); when both an operational spec and a set-level spec exist, is each
   justified; is bound narrowing (`PartialOrd` vs `Ord` plus obeying-laws `requires`)
   principled and are redundant `requires` conjuncts flagged (check the vstd law definitions
   — one conjunct may imply the others); are type-level properties independent of irrelevant
   value arguments, and well-formedness predicates made methods when they describe one
   model. For indexing: `Seq::spec_index` is total with unspecified out-of-bounds values,
   so spec helpers may rely on that, but a property needing a valid index keeps bounds and
   explicit triggers; executable indexing still needs non-panicking bounds (`requires` or
   `IndexSpec::index_req`), and a model of executable `get` preserves `Option`
   success/failure semantics — unspecified spec values do not replace that contract. For
   quantifiers: prefer standard predicates such as `Seq::all` (their predicate-based
   triggers can reduce spurious instantiations vs broad index triggers like `s[i]`), use a
   subrange predicate when it reads better, and do not add an axiom for a fact derivable
   from the sequence definition.
7. Invariant modeling (`implement-inv-for-models`). When the target defines spec structs,
   check whether intrinsic validity is expressed as an `impl Inv` through `inv()` rather
   than a stand-alone `wf(...)` predicate, applying the pure-spec distinction below.
   The guideline reserves `wf(...)` for relationships depending on another value;
   distinguish that naming convention from a claim that a validity condition is
   redundant. Require `inv()` before operations that assume a valid state and ensure
   it after those that promise to preserve it (`old(self).inv()` /
   `final(self).inv()` for mutable operations). Private fields give representation hiding
   but do not make Verus establish `inv()` automatically; when no intrinsic invariant
   applies, record N/A with the reason.
   Before proposing removal of `wf`/`inv` because a type has a `type_invariant`,
   classify its consumers by mode. Type invariants apply to exec and tracked objects,
   not arbitrary spec values, quantified variables, or values selected from spec
   collections. `use_type_invariant` needs an exec/tracked variable; a broadcast lemma
   requiring `type_inv(x)` only exports consequences after that premise is established.
   It cannot manufacture validity for a spec-only `x`. Explicit validity predicates
   may therefore coexist with type invariants to serve pure-spec invariants and
   quantified conditions. Report redundancy only when every affected consumer can
   obtain the same facts through a legal proof path; never remove a spec premise merely
   because exec/tracked callers obtain it implicitly. Check the active
   `source/docs/guide/src/reference-type-invariants.md` and the
   [acknowledged PR #860 correction](https://github.com/asterinas/vostd/pull/860#discussion_r4396558740).
   For changed resource-accounting models, identify the promised accounting invariant
   or clean-boundary guarantee, then trace token creation, transfer and redemption
   against ghost bookkeeping. Check whether a legal caller can reset the ledger while
   retaining an outstanding tracked token and falsely establish that guarantee.
   Inspect field visibility, mutation access and the relationship linking entries to
   tokens. Neither an unrelated `inv()` nor privacy alone establishes conservation;
   require a concrete bypass of the promised property, not a particular ledger design.
   Compare with the base to isolate newly exposed bypasses. Report a broken accounting
   guarantee without claiming a runtime memory error or logical contradiction unless
   separately demonstrated.

You own contract completeness, trust placement, and model reuse — not documentation
phrasing (Maintainability persona), the `rlimit > 200` threshold, or whether a changed
standard-library external spec should be proposed upstream (Workflow persona).
The Specification persona separately audits API precondition permissiveness and
caller-visible postcondition sufficiency, including natural-client checks. Keep this
pass focused on external-model soundness, vacuity, and proof/model engineering;
return overlapping evidence for consolidation rather than duplicating its API audit.

personas/maintainability.md.text:
# Maintainability persona

**Review section:** High/Medium/Low findings on shape, layout, and documentation
**Remit:** Can the next reader see what runs, what models the mathematics,
and what exists only to prove something — without archaeology?

**Your guideline page (the authority — read it in full first):**
`docs/coding-guidelines/maintainability.md`

Open the page now and enumerate every rule it currently contains, by kebab-case short
name. Check every one of them against the target; the page outranks everything below.
If the page has rules this list does not name, review them through the closest method
below; if a rule named below no longer exists on the page, drop it.

**Concerns, in order:**

1. Take the page's current rule list as your checklist; clear every rule with a finding
   or an explicit compliance note citing line references.
2. Executable shape (`preserve-exec-code`): recover the original executable code from
   `git log -p` and the upstream history. Flag moved items, rewritten expressions whose
   original form is not shown in the change, and equivalences that cannot be checked from
   the review text alone. Flag reversed conversion lemmas, reconstructed values, runtime
   clones, and caller-facing API changes introduced only to ease a proof. Flag prose
   comments added onto executable code that state neither a verified property nor a
   caller-facing trust boundary (comment freezing), and an executable call replaced by a
   differently packaged equivalent when the original callee lacked a specification — the
   page requires specifying the original callee first, with a record of the concrete
   obstacle when the call is still replaced. When Verus
   forces an executable change, it must stay minimal and the original form must be shown
   in the review; hold it to whichever comment format the page currently mandates.
   Inspect deleted original-code comments as well as added markers. Distinguish a
   missing provenance comment from changed behavior: documenting a rewrite does not
   restore evaluation order or panic diagnostics. Check restored markers against
   available history; an unchanged body in this patch does not disprove a prior rewrite.
3. Mode separation and layout (`separate-verus-modes`): executable code, specifications,
   and proofs sit in visually distinct groups, and adjacent verified items share one
   `verus!` block when no ordinary Rust item separates them.
4. Proof-body hygiene, mapping each check to its rule:
   - `organize-proof-imports` / `group-imports-by-crate`: audit `reveal`,
     `reveal_with_fuel`, and `broadcast use` for repeated long paths that an import would
     replace, and combine same-crate definitions within each guideline-defined import
     group, even across modules. Retain a qualified path only where the page permits — ambiguity or a one-off
     reference — and keep `reveal`/`reveal_with_fuel` minimal. A `reveal` of an `open` spec
     fn is still load-bearing, so remove one only when verification stays green, and leave a
     one-line note on a non-obvious `reveal` or fuel value that must remain.
     Check redundant qualification against imports already in scope, accounting for
     aliases and shadowing. Apply grouping rules separately to verification-added
     imports and inherited executable imports where the guideline distinguishes them.
   - `use-chained-comparisons`: contiguous bounds that share intermediate expressions are
     one chained comparison, in contracts, invariants, predicates, and assertions — but
     only where the chain is logically equivalent and no relation is invented or contract
     strengthened to form it.
   - `use-returns-for-exact-results`: exact return values use `returns expr` (type-matched,
     with required casts such as `as usize` kept and justified); unused named binders and
     `-> (ret: ())` declarations are removed.
   - `bind-option-payloads`: two or more facts over the same `Option` bind the payload once
     with `matches` and group the facts in one implication; leave a lone implication
     ungrouped when binding would not aid clarity. Preserve whether `Some` is required:
     `x matches Some(v) ==> P(v)` is true for `None`, so it cannot by itself replace
     `x is Some` together with payload constraints. Keep the presence requirement or
     use a match whose `None` arm is false. See the corrected suggestion in
     [PR #860](https://github.com/asterinas/vostd/pull/860#discussion_r4392170062).
   - `qualified-verus-spec-calls`: a `#[verus_spec(...)]` call site uses a qualified path
     when an import would block Verus from finding the specification, rather than adding an
     import solely to change resolution.
   - `match-enum-results`: check whether one stated direction already follows from
     the remaining clauses and enum exhaustiveness. Recommend removal only after
     establishing logical equivalence, preserving success/failure conditions and
     payload facts; an Err/None clause may carry independent guarantees.
5. Naming and modes (`name-proof-roles`, `avoid-redundant-mode-markers`,
   `prefer-ghost-model-structs`): `lemma_`/`tracked_`/`axiom_` prefixes and resource names
   that state their ownership role; `ghost`/`tracked`/plain mode chosen deliberately per
   struct and confirmed by verification (`ghost struct` first for proof-only models and
   zero-sized generic arguments, `tracked struct` for linear permissions, plain struct for
   runtime state); markers used only where they communicate or enforce a mode boundary,
   with `tracked_`/`ghost_` field prefixes inside executable types and no redundant marker
   repeated on every field of a `ghost struct`.
   Include unit-returning proof helpers that manipulate tracked ownership when
   applying `tracked_` naming. Classify their role from signatures and uses; a tracked
   parameter alone does not make an executable API an ownership proof helper.
6. Documentation (`document-verified-apis`): preserve original runtime docs. For a public
   executable API, append a `Verified Properties` section — `Safety` (classes of undefined
   behavior ruled out, any proved absence of panic, and remaining trusted boundaries,
   claiming only what verification establishes), `Functional Correctness` when applicable,
   `Preconditions`, and `Postconditions`. A proved absence of panic is a `Safety` claim,
   not a `Postconditions` one. Each field states only nontrivial content: a clause
   evident from the function's name, signature, ordinary rustdoc, or the type's
   invariant — one restating the spec, the summary line, or the signature — is dropped,
   not enumerated; a field with nothing to state is omitted; a contract whose only
   further clause is the proved absence of panic is a single `## Safety` line. For a
   `spec fn`, document the
   mathematical meaning of the value it denotes; for a `proof fn`, one sentence summarizing
   the proved fact, with further prose only for a non-obvious obligation or guarantee. Do
   **not** add `Preconditions`/`Postconditions` to spec or proof functions — their
   `requires`/`ensures` clauses already state those formally. A verified module gets a
   `Verified Properties` paragraph covering verification design, critical invariants,
   safety, and verified functional correctness. A documentation finding reports only a
   misleading gap — wrong or missing text that would misstate verified behavior or a
   trust boundary. Completeness nits (enumerating trivial clauses, bullet count versus
   clause count, retrofitting
   module-level prose onto code whose verification grew in the diff, wording polish) are
   `Compliance` notes, not findings.
7. Placement (`right-size-spec-placement`): grep the repo for users of each spec fn the
   target defines; a small model beside its single user is correct, a shared or growing
   model belongs under `ostd/specs/`. Executable-code comments are otherwise frozen with
   the code: do not request supplementary rustdoc or narrative comments on executable
   code beyond verified-property or trust-boundary statements and `Origin Rust:` rewrite
   markers (see the page's `preserve-exec-code` section).
   For `defer-auxiliary-proof-functions`, use visibility and consumers to distinguish
   exported proof/model APIs and critical proofs from private auxiliary lemmas.
   Keep APIs and critical proofs first; defer only lemmas serving side obligations,
   not every private proof function.
8. Debt and lint (`document-real-proof-debt`, `narrow-lint-suppressions`): proof comments
   tied to current, non-obvious constraints and their consequences; shared trust boundaries
   documented once at module level; a `TODO` for temporary limitations needing follow-up; no
   restating of code or speculation about tool limits. Flag a doc claim whose supporting
   assert a later commit removed (`git log -p` tells). Lints suppressed at the smallest
   item or expression scope, preferring `#[expect(...)]` for deliberately triggered lints
   over crate- or module-wide `allow`.

You own readability and structure, not contract completeness or proof reuse
(Proof-engineering persona), the `rlimit > 200` threshold, or whether a changed
standard-library external spec should be proposed upstream (Workflow persona).
